$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x)
$$

is regular if both $(x-a)P(x)$ and $(x-a)^{2}Q(x)$ are analytic about $x=a.$ Otherwise, the singular point is irregular.

First, we rewrite the differential equation in standard form by dividing by $(x-1):$

$$

$$

So, we have

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{and}\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{(x-1)^{3}}.
$$

Let's now check each statement in turn.

- Since the denominators of both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ vanish at $x=1,$ they are *not* analytic about $x=1.$ So, statement I is false.

$$
(x-1)P(x)=(x-1)\frac{1}{x-1}=1
$$

is analytic about $x=1,$ while the function

$$
(x-1)^{2}Q(x)=(x-1)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{(x-1)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x-1}
$$
